screens.title: Configuration Space and Graph Search
screens.subtitle: Transform geometry into search: from workspace obstacles to graph-based motion planning

narration.text: Motion planning asks a very practical question: given a robot, a start, a goal, and obstacles, how do we compute a collision-free path? The key trick we use is to change perspectives. Instead of reasoning about the robot shape moving through a room, we build a configuration space — a space of all possible robot poses — where the robot becomes a point and obstacles become regions to avoid. This transformation converts geometric collision checking into a graph search problem we can solve with standard algorithms. In this chapter you will learn how to construct C-obstacles, build graphs or grids over C-space, and apply Breadth-First Search, Dijkstra, and A* to find valid paths. You will see how heuristics guide search behavior, why admissibility matters, and how complexity grows with grid resolution and dimensionality. A concrete outcome of this lesson is a hands-on MATLAB experiment: implement A* on a 50 by 50 grid with random obstacles, compare it to Dijkstra, and observe how a good heuristic can drastically reduce explored nodes. Think about your own robot: what degrees of freedom determine its C-space, and how would that shape the planning method you choose?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: By mapping robot poses into a configuration space, planning becomes a pathfinding problem for a point that avoids C-obstacles — enabling BFS, Dijkstra, and A* to compute collision-free motions.

Practical note
Higher-dimensional robots produce high-dimensional C-spaces, so planners often use discretized graphs or sampling methods to remain tractable.

screens.title: Configuration Space (C-space)
screens.subtitle: What C-space is and why it simplifies motion planning

narration.text: Configuration space is the set of all possible robot configurations or poses. For a simple mobile robot that can translate and rotate on a plane, a configuration is (x, y, theta). For a robot arm, a configuration is a tuple of joint angles. The advantage of C-space is conceptual clarity: the robot is treated as a point, and obstacles in the workspace become regions in C-space where that point is not allowed. This reduces collision reasoning to a pathfinding problem. A concrete example: a circular robot of radius r navigating around a table. In workspace, the robot is a disk; in C-space the table's obstacles are grown by r so the point representing the robot cannot enter those expanded regions. A common misconception is to confuse workspace coordinates with configuration coordinates; they are equal only when the robot is a point. Another subtlety is that orientation expands C-space dimensionality: adding theta increases complexity because obstacles depend on orientation for non-circular robots. Key takeaway: modeling the correct C-space is the most important step—get it wrong and even an optimal planner will return an invalid path. Consider your robot now: which degrees of freedom are essential, and how do they change the dimension and structure of its C-space?

keyIdea.title: C-space essence
keyIdea.text: C-space turns a robot into a point in a space of poses; obstacles become forbidden regions determined by robot geometry and orientation.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Configuration Space (C-space)
Definition and intuition
The configuration space is the set of all robot poses. Use it to map collision checking into pathfinding for a point.
Concrete example
A circular mobile robot of radius r: expand workspace obstacles by r and plan for a point.
Misconception
C-space is not the same as workspace unless the robot is a point. Orientation and joint angles create extra dimensions.
Why this matters
A correct C-space makes collision checking local and lets you reuse graph search algorithms for planning.
Key Takeaway

Modeling the right degrees of freedom and representing obstacles in C-space is the foundational step for any motion planner.

Quick reference
Common C-spaces:
  • Point robot in 2D: (x, y)
  • Circular robot in 2D: (x, y, theta) but obstacles expanded by radius
  • 6-joint arm: (theta1, theta2, ..., theta6)
Short notation
Point mobile robot: C = { (x, y) }
Circular robot: C = { (x, y, θ) }
6-DOF arm: C = { (θ1, θ2, θ3, θ4, θ5, θ6) }
Remember: dimensionality grows quickly with degrees of freedom, making naive grids intractable for many manipulators.

screens.title: Converting workspace obstacles to C-obstacles
screens.subtitle: Minkowski sum and swept volume concepts

narration.text: Turning workspace obstacles into C-obstacles makes collision checking straightforward. For simple circular robots the operation is intuitive: compute the Minkowski sum of each obstacle with a disk of radius equal to the robot radius. This expands obstacles so that if a point representing the robot enters any expanded region, the real robot would collide. For polygonal robots or arms that rotate, we must account for orientation: compute swept volumes as the robot rotates or moves along a simple motion, and mark all configurations that produce intersections. A concrete example is a rectangular robot that can rotate; its C-obstacle depends on both position and orientation, and computing it exactly requires rotating the rectangle and taking the union of occupied workspace. A common misinterpretation is to expand only the robot and not the obstacles; Minkowski sum is symmetric in this context, but in practice we usually expand obstacles by the robot shape because it is simpler. Practical planners often approximate C-obstacles by conservative expansions or by sampling collision checks when exact geometry is expensive. The main takeaway: representing collisions correctly in C-space is essential for planner safety and correctness.

keyIdea.title: Obstacle mapping
keyIdea.text: Use Minkowski expansion for simple shapes; use swept volumes or conservative approximations for rotating and articulated robots to build safe C-obstacles.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › C-obstacles & Minkowski
From workspace to C-obstacles
Apply Minkowski expansion or swept-volume reasoning to mark forbidden configurations for the robot point.
Minkowski sum (circular robot)
Expand each workspace obstacle by the robot radius. The robot reduces to a point and must avoid expanded areas.
Swept volume (rotating/polygonal)
Union the workspace area occupied by the robot across relevant orientations or motions to mark forbidden configurations.
Common mistake
Assuming obstacle expansion is negligible. For non-circular robots orientation changes the shape of C-obstacles significantly.
Key Takeaway

Compute C-obstacles conservatively when exact geometry is expensive; correctness is more important than tightness for safety.

Illustrative steps
  1. Model robot shape (disk, rectangle, polygon).
  2. If disk: inflate obstacles by radius (Minkowski).
  3. If polygonal/rotating: compute sweeps over orientation samples or conservative envelope.
  4. Mark grid cells or configurations whose robot shape intersects any workspace obstacle.
These steps produce a binary occupancy indication in C-space used to build graphs or to reject sampled configurations during planning.

screens.title: Graph representation of C-space
screens.subtitle: Grids, nodes, edges, and collision-free connectivity

narration.text: Once we have a C-space with forbidden regions marked, we must choose a representation for search. A common and clear choice is a discretized grid: divide C-space into cells, mark cells as free or occupied, and connect neighboring free cells with edges. Each cell becomes a node in a graph; edges represent feasible small motions between configurations. For mobile robots in 2D, 4-connected or 8-connected grids are typical. For higher-dimensional C-spaces, grids quickly explode in size, so planners either use coarse discretization or sampling-based graphs. A concrete scenario: a 50 by 50 grid represents 2,500 vertices; with 4-connected neighbors, edges are about 10,000. This is easy for BFS, Dijkstra, or A*. A common misconception is that finer grids always give better paths — they can, but they also increase computation and may require smoothing afterward. Key practical choices include connectivity (4 vs 8 neighbors), cost assignment for edges (uniform, distance-based), and whether to store occupancy per cell or per node. The takeaway: choose the representation that balances path quality and computational resources for your robot's operational needs. Graph representation of C-space means discretize c-space into nodes and edges; decide connectivity and edge costs to trade off path quality against computational cost.. In practical terms, grids, nodes, edges, and collision-free connectivity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Graph model
keyIdea.text: Discretize C-space into nodes and edges; decide connectivity and edge costs to trade off path quality against computational cost.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Graph representation
Grid to graph
Discretize C-space into cells and link free cells to create a graph for search.
Connectivity choices: 4-connected (N,E,S,W) or 8-connected (diagonals allowed). Edge cost may be uniform or equal to Euclidean distance between cell centers.
Practical note: A fine grid improves path fidelity but raises V and E, increasing memory and run time.
Key Takeaway

Select grid resolution and connectivity to match robot accuracy requirements and available compute, and be ready to smooth paths afterward.

Example counts
For a 50×50 grid: V = 2500 nodes. With 4 neighbors per cell, E ≈ 4V. These magnitudes guide algorithm choice.
Edge costs
# Uniform cost: cost = 1 for each neighbor
# Distance cost: cost = Euclidean distance between cell centers
Label nodes with occupancy and store parent pointers during search to reconstruct the final path.

screens.title: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
screens.subtitle: Unweighted shortest paths and uniform expansion

narration.text: Breadth-First Search explores nodes in order of increasing number of edges from the start. It is the right choice on unweighted graphs when the goal is the fewest-edge path. BFS uses a queue and marks nodes visited as it enqueues them. A concrete example: on a 4-connected grid where every move has equal cost, BFS will find the shortest path measured in steps. A common limitation is memory: BFS stores entire frontiers and visited sets, which can be large for fine grids. Also, BFS is not suitable for weighted edges — it ignores edge costs and could produce a suboptimal path when edge costs differ. The provided MATLAB style pseudocode illustrates typical structure: enqueue start, loop until queue empty, dequeue current, check goal, and enqueue unseen neighbors while recording parents. After the search, reconstruct the path by following parent pointers from goal back to start. Takeaway: BFS is simple and guaranteed to find shortest paths in unweighted graphs, but be mindful of memory and edge-cost assumptions. Breadth-First Search (BFS) means bfs finds the fewest-step path on unweighted graphs by expanding layers uniformly; it is simple but memory-intensive.. In practical terms, unweighted shortest paths and uniform expansion. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: BFS summary
keyIdea.text: BFS finds the fewest-step path on unweighted graphs by expanding layers uniformly; it is simple but memory-intensive.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Breadth-First Search
BFS overview
Use BFS for unweighted grids to guarantee fewest-step paths.
• Uses a FIFO queue and a visited set to avoid repeats.
• Guarantees shortest path in number of edges on unweighted graphs.
• Memory grows with the frontier size; be cautious for large grids.
• Not appropriate when edges have non-uniform costs; use Dijkstra or A* instead.
Key Takeaway

BFS is reliable and simple for uniform-cost grids but becomes costly in memory as grid size grows.

MATLAB-style pseudocode
function path = bfs(graph, start, goal)
  queue = {start};
  visited = containers.Map();
  visited(mat2str(start)) = true;
  parent = containers.Map();
  while ~isempty(queue)
    current = queue{1}; queue(1) = [];
    if isequal(current, goal)
      path = reconstruct_path(parent, start, goal);
      return;
    end
    for neighbor = graph.neighbors(current)
      if ~visited.isKey(mat2str(neighbor))
        visited(mat2str(neighbor)) = true;
        parent(mat2str(neighbor)) = current;
        queue{end+1} = neighbor;
      end
    end
  end
  path = [];
end
Reconstruct the final path by following parent pointers back from goal to start; this is standard in grid planners.

screens.title: Dijkstra's Algorithm
screens.subtitle: Weighted shortest paths using a priority queue

narration.text: Dijkstra's algorithm generalizes BFS to weighted graphs where edges have non-uniform costs. It maintains a priority queue keyed by tentative distance from the start and repeatedly extracts the node with smallest distance, relaxing its outgoing edges. A concrete example: if diagonal moves in a grid are more expensive than orthogonal moves, Dijkstra computes the true shortest-cost path considering these costs. Unlike BFS, Dijkstra guarantees optimality for weighted graphs. A typical misconception is that Dijkstra is always slower than A*; Dijkstra explores in all directions but is optimal when no heuristic information is available or when you need full shortest paths to multiple targets. Complexity with a binary heap or similar priority queue is O((V + E) log V) time and O(V) space. In practice, Dijkstra can be used as a baseline by setting the heuristic to zero in A*, which shows the direct relationship between the two algorithms. Takeaway: use Dijkstra when edge costs matter and admissible heuristics are not available or when you need full shortest-distance information from a source. Dijkstra's Algorithm means dijkstra finds optimal paths in weighted graphs using a priority queue; it explores broadly and is the baseline for weighted shortest-path planning.. In practical terms, weighted shortest paths using a priority queue. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Dijkstra core
keyIdea.text: Dijkstra finds optimal paths in weighted graphs using a priority queue; it explores broadly and is the baseline for weighted shortest-path planning.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Dijkstra
Dijkstra overview
Find shortest-cost paths on weighted graphs using a priority queue keyed by distance.
• Maintains tentative distance g(n) for each node and a parent map.
• Extracts the node with smallest g and relaxes neighbors until target is reached.
• Optimal for non-negative edge costs; performance depends on V and E.
• Use as a baseline by running A* with a zero heuristic.
Key Takeaway

Dijkstra is the correct choice for weighted pathfinding when heuristic information is unavailable or when absolute optimality is required.

Algorithm sketch
# Dijkstra core behavior
initialize distances g(start)=0, others = inf
priority queue ordered by g
while queue not empty:
  current = pop min g
  if current is goal: reconstruct path
  for neighbor in neighbors(current):
    tentative = g(current) + cost(current,neighbor)
    if tentative < g(neighbor):
      g(neighbor) = tentative
      parent(neighbor) = current
      insert or decrease-key neighbor in queue
Remember to use a priority queue implementation to achieve the stated time bound; otherwise performance can degrade.

screens.title: A* (A-Star) Algorithm
screens.subtitle: Heuristic-guided search for efficient optimal planning

narration.text: A* extends Dijkstra by adding a heuristic estimate h(n) of the remaining cost to the goal and prioritizing nodes by f(n) = g(n) + h(n). If the heuristic is admissible — meaning it never overestimates true cost — A* is guaranteed to find an optimal path. If the heuristic is also consistent (it satisfies the triangle inequality), A* is optimally efficient for that heuristic: no other algorithm using the same heuristic will expand fewer nodes and still guarantee optimality. A concrete example is a grid where h is Euclidean distance to the goal; A* will be pulled toward the goal and explore fewer nodes than Dijkstra. A common misconception is that a heuristic with higher numeric values is always better; if the heuristic overestimates, you may find a suboptimal path. The safe rule is admissibility for optimality and consistency for implementation simplicity. Takeaway: use A* with admissible heuristics when you need optimality and performance, and choose heuristics that reflect the geometry of your problem. A* (A-Star) Algorithm means a* balances known cost and heuristic estimate to prioritize promising nodes; admissible heuristics preserve optimality while reducing explored nodes.. In practical terms, heuristic-guided search for efficient optimal planning. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: A* core
keyIdea.text: A* balances known cost and heuristic estimate to prioritize promising nodes; admissible heuristics preserve optimality while reducing explored nodes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › A* Algorithm
A* in brief
Combine the path cost so far with a goal estimate to guide search efficiently.
• Uses f(n) = g(n) + h(n) to order the open set.
• If h is admissible, A* finds an optimal path.
• If h is consistent, implementation can avoid reprocessing nodes and remains efficient.
• A* often explores far fewer nodes than Dijkstra with a good heuristic.
Key Takeaway

Admissible heuristics let A* remain optimal while focusing exploration; choose heuristics that reflect true geometric cost when possible.

Heuristic examples
• Euclidean distance: admissible for continuous movement, encourages straight paths.
• Manhattan distance: admissible on 4-connected grids and when movements are axis-aligned.
• Zero heuristic: reduces A* to Dijkstra, exploring broadly but safely.
Carefully test heuristics on your grid: a heuristic that overestimates can speed up runtime but sacrifices optimality, which is usually unacceptable for critical robot tasks.

screens.title: Common heuristics: Euclidean vs Manhattan vs Zero
screens.subtitle: How heuristics influence search behavior and admissibility

narration.text: Choosing a heuristic is a balance between guidance and admissibility. Euclidean distance estimates straight-line distance to the goal and is admissible on grids where movement cost matches or exceeds straight-line distance, making it useful for continuous or 8-connected grids. Manhattan distance — the sum of absolute axis differences — is admissible on 4-connected grids where moves are limited to axis directions. The zero heuristic is admissible by definition and makes A* behave exactly like Dijkstra. A concrete example: on a 4-connected grid with only orthogonal moves, Euclidean heuristic may slightly underestimate the true path cost but remains admissible; however Manhattan is tighter and can give stronger guidance. A misconception is that a larger heuristic value always reduces explored nodes; if it overestimates the true cost, A* can produce suboptimal paths. The practical rule is: pick the heuristic that reflects your motion model and preserves admissibility. When in doubt, run both heuristics and measure nodes explored and final path cost to evaluate tradeoffs. Common heuristics: Euclidean vs Manhattan vs Zero means pick a heuristic that matches motion connectivity: euclidean for continuous or diagonal moves, manhattan for axis-aligned moves, and zero when no admissible heuristic is available.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Heuristic selection
keyIdea.text: Pick a heuristic that matches motion connectivity: Euclidean for continuous or diagonal moves, Manhattan for axis-aligned moves, and zero when no admissible heuristic is available.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Heuristic Comparison
Heuristics at a glance
Each heuristic encodes assumptions about allowed motion and cost structure.
Euclidean
Straight-line distance; admissible and effective for diagonal and continuous moves.
Manhattan
Sum of axis differences; tight for 4-connected grids with axis-aligned moves.
Zero
No guidance; A* reduces to Dijkstra. Safe but may explore broadly.
Key Takeaway

Match your heuristic to the motion model; tighter admissible heuristics usually reduce exploration while preserving optimality.

Concrete example
On a 4-connected grid: Manhattan distance often yields fewer explored nodes than Euclidean because it better matches allowed moves. On an 8-connected grid, Euclidean typically performs better.
Measure explored-node counts in your experiments to confirm which heuristic is best for your map and connectivity. Practical tuning and measurement beat guesswork.

screens.title: Time and space complexity analysis
screens.subtitle: Cost bounds for BFS, Dijkstra, and A* on discrete grids

narration.text: Understanding complexity helps choose between planners. BFS runs in O(V + E) time and O(V) space because it explores edges and nodes layer by layer; on an n by n grid V = n squared and E is about 4V for 4-connected grids. Dijkstra with a binary heap runs in O((V + E) log V) time and O(V) space due to priority queue operations. A* has the same worst-case complexity as Dijkstra — O((V + E) log V) — but in practice with a good admissible heuristic it explores far fewer nodes, making it much faster on typical maps. For example, on a 50 by 50 grid, V=2500 and E≈10000; these numbers fit comfortably in memory and allow fast searches. A notable misconception is treating average-case performance as worst-case guarantees; while A* is often faster, its worst-case behavior still matches Dijkstra if the heuristic provides no guidance. The practical takeaway: analyze your grid resolution, connectivity, and available memory, and then pick the search algorithm and heuristic accordingly. Time and space complexity analysis means bfs: o(v+e) time, o(v) space. dijkstra/a*: o((v+e) log v) time with a priority queue; a* often faster in practice with a good admissible heuristic.. In practical terms, cost bounds for bfs, dijkstra, and a* on discrete grids. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Complexity summary
keyIdea.text: BFS: O(V+E) time, O(V) space. Dijkstra/A*: O((V+E) log V) time with a priority queue; A* often faster in practice with a good admissible heuristic.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Complexity Analysis
Algorithmic bounds
Relate V and E on grids to expected time and memory.
• BFS: time O(V + E), space O(V). Works for unweighted graphs.
• Dijkstra: time O((V + E) log V) with a heap, space O(V). Handles weights.
• A*: worst-case O((V + E) log V) but often far fewer expansions with a good heuristic.
Key Takeaway

Estimate V and E from grid resolution before choosing a planner. For many mobile robot tasks, A* with an appropriate heuristic is the practical sweet spot.

Grid example
50×50 grid: V = 2,500. With 4-connected neighbors, E ≈ 10,000. These sizes are trivial for modern machines, but grids that represent high-dimensional manipulators become infeasible quickly.
If memory is limited, consider coarser discretization, hierarchical planning, or sampling-based planners that avoid full grid enumeration.

screens.title: Dimensionality and robot geometry
screens.subtitle: How DOFs and shape affect planner choices

narration.text: Robot degrees of freedom and geometry fundamentally shape planner design. A planar mobile robot with position and orientation yields a three-dimensional C-space, while a six-joint arm produces a six-dimensional C-space. Each added degree of freedom multiplies the size of a naive grid representation, making dense discretization infeasible. For robots with few DOFs, grid-based A* is practical and interpretable. For high-DOF manipulators, sampling-based planners or variants that plan in task-space and then refine joint-space trajectories become necessary. A concrete example: a 6-DOF arm using a joint-angle grid with even modest resolution per joint produces enormous vertex counts, so practitioners prefer sampling or hierarchical approaches. A common misconception is that more accurate geometric collision models always require finer grids; often a hybrid approach works better: coarse graph search plus local continuous collision checks and smoothing. The takeaway is to match your representation and algorithm to robot complexity—use grid-based A* where degrees of freedom are low and sampling or specialized planners when dimensionality rises. Dimensionality and robot geometry means match planner representation to robot dofs: grid-based search for low-dof systems; sampling or hierarchical methods for high-dof manipulators.. In practical terms, how dofs and shape affect planner choices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practical rule
keyIdea.text: Match planner representation to robot DOFs: grid-based search for low-DOF systems; sampling or hierarchical methods for high-DOF manipulators.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Dimensionality & Geometry
Degrees of freedom matter
Higher DOFs increase state-space size and change planner feasibility.
• Low DOF (mobile base): grid-based A* is practical and fast.
• High DOF (manipulator): joint-space grids explode; prefer sampling or hierarchical approaches.
• Geometry matters: circular robots allow simple expansions; articulated robots need swept-volume or collision checking per configuration.
Key Takeaway

Plan in the simplest representation that captures necessary motion constraints; avoid unnecessarily high-resolution discretization for high-DOF systems.

Design checklist
  • List robot DOFs and decide which are essential for your task.
  • Decide representation: grid, sampling, or hybrid.
  • Choose collision modeling fidelity: conservative expansion vs exact swept volumes.
This checklist helps you balance safety, path quality, and computational cost when designing a planner for a specific robot and task.

screens.title: MATLAB A* experiment
screens.subtitle: Implement A*, visualize results, and compare to Dijkstra

narration.text: This exercise translates theory into measurable results. Implement A* on a 50 by 50 grid with twenty percent random obstacles. Set start at (5,5) and goal at (45,45). Use a Euclidean heuristic for A*, and then run Dijkstra by replacing the heuristic with zero. Key Takeaway

Empirical measurement over random trials demonstrates practical benefits of a good heuristic and surfaces variance in planning difficulty.

Starter pseudocode
function [path, explored] = astar(grid, start, goal, heuristic)
  open = PriorityQueue();
  open.insert(start, heuristic(start, goal));
  g = containers.Map(); g(mat2str(start)) = 0;
  parent = containers.Map();
  explored = [];
  while ~open.isEmpty()
    current = open.pop();
    explored(end+1,:) = current;
    if isequal(current, goal)
      path = reconstruct_path(parent, start, goal); return;
    end
    for nb = grid.neighbors(current)
      tentative = g(mat2str(current)) + grid.cost(current, nb);
      if ~g.isKey(mat2str(nb)) || tentative < g(mat2str(nb))
        g(mat2str(nb)) = tentative;
        f = tentative + heuristic(nb, goal);
        open.insert(nb, f);
        parent(mat2str(nb)) = current;
      end
    end
  end
  path = []; 
end
Use a consistent random seed when debugging, but vary seeds across trials when measuring average behavior. Visualize explored nodes to build intuition about algorithmic differences.
